question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Throw cold water on
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. To show indifference.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Throw cold water on" means to discourage someone or to dampen enthusiasm for a plan or idea by showing indifference or disapproval towards it. (किसी के प्रति उदासीनता दिखाकर हतोत्साहित करना)
◦ Example: Whenever I suggest a new project at work, my manager throws cold water on it.

• The expression pictures the literal act of throwing cold water on a fire or on someone's enthusiasm to dampen or extinguish it, just as real cold water would put out flames.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: To rinse thoroughly — this is only the literal, non-idiomatic sense of washing something with water; it carries no figurative meaning of discouragement.

• Option 3: To encourage (प्रोत्साहित करना) — this is the opposite of the idiom's actual meaning; "throw cold water on" always carries a negative, discouraging sense.

• Option 4: To talk nicely — unrelated to the idiom; it describes polite speech, not discouragement.

NOTE

• Other idioms of discouragement/negativity often asked in SSC: "To pour cold water on" (same meaning as this idiom), "To rain on someone's parade" (to spoil someone's happiness or plans) and "To put a damper on" (to reduce enthusiasm).

• Contrast with idioms of encouragement: "To give a pat on the back" (to praise) and "To give the green signal" (to approve).

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
Unpleasantly rough or sharp, especially to the senses, cruel
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Harsh.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Harsh" means unpleasantly rough or sharp, especially to the senses; cruel or severe in manner. (कठोर, कर्कश)
◦ Example: The harsh winter wind cut through their thin jackets.

• Harsh can describe sounds (a harsh voice), climate (harsh weather), treatment (harsh punishment), or light/colour (harsh lighting) — anything unpleasantly severe to the senses or feelings.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Haslet (हैसलेट) — a dish of pig's offal (liver, heart, etc.) cooked together; a culinary term unrelated to harshness.

• Option 2: Hart (हिरन) — an adult male deer, a completely unrelated animal-noun.

• Option 4: Hasp (कड़ी/चटकनी) — a metal fastening device (a hinged metal plate) used with a padlock to fasten a door; unrelated in meaning.

NOTE

• These four words (Haslet, Hart, Harsh, Hasp) are commonly confused in SSC spelling/vocabulary sets because of their similar spelling pattern ("Ha_s_").

• Synonyms of "harsh": severe, stern, grating, abrasive, rough. Antonyms: mild, gentle, soft, soothing.

question:
Select the ANTONYM of the word inadvertent to fill in the blank.
Everyone likes to speak in a clear and ________ manner.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. deliberate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "inadvertent" means unintentional; done without conscious thought or by accident. (अनजाने में किया गया)

• Its antonym is "deliberate", meaning done consciously and intentionally, after careful thought. (जानबूझकर किया गया)
◦ Example: Everyone likes to speak in a clear and deliberate manner.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: unintentional (अनजाने में) — this is a synonym, not an antonym, of "inadvertent"; it means the opposite of what is required here.

• Option 2: peevish (चिड़चिड़ा) — means irritable or easily annoyed; unrelated to the intentional/unintentional distinction.

• Option 4: impious (अधार्मिक) — means lacking respect or reverence, especially in religious matters; unrelated in meaning.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "inadvertent": accidental, unplanned, unwitting, careless.

• Other synonyms of "deliberate": intentional, calculated, premeditated, purposeful — frequently tested as antonym pairs in SSC vocabulary sections.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Syamala is more taller than her sister.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Syamala is taller than her sister.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "Syamala is more taller than her sister" contains a double comparative error — both "more" and the "-er" suffix (in "taller") are used together to form the comparative degree, which is grammatically incorrect.

• Rule — Comparative Degree: A comparative degree is formed either by adding "-er" to a short (one or two-syllable) adjective, or by placing "more" before a longer adjective — never both at the same time.
◦ Correct: tall → taller (not "more taller")
◦ Correct: beautiful → more beautiful (not "more beautifuller")

• Applying the rule, the redundant "more" must be dropped, leaving simply "taller": Syamala is taller than her sister.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "tall" is the positive degree, not the comparative degree required when two people are being compared with "than".

• Option 3: "most taller" repeats the same double-comparison error by combining "most" (superlative marker) with "-er" (comparative marker).

• Option 4: "tallest" is the superlative degree, used to compare three or more people, not two; here only two people (Syamala and her sister) are being compared, so the comparative "taller" is needed, not the superlative.

NOTE

• A comparison between exactly two persons/things always takes the comparative degree + than; a comparison among three or more always takes the superlative degree + the + adjective + of/in.

• Common double-comparative errors to watch for: "more better", "more easier", "most best", "most tallest" — all incorrect for the same reason.

question:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error from the given options. If you don't find any error, mark 'No error' as your answer.
Hurray! Here is the toy / what I was looking for / as my birthday gift.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. what I was looking for.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The segment "what I was looking for" is incorrect because the relative pronoun "what" is used, even though the sentence already has a clear antecedent — "the toy".

• Rule — Relative Pronouns: "What" is used only when there is no antecedent (it means "that which"); when an antecedent noun is already present, the relative pronoun "that" or "which" must be used instead.

• Since "the toy" is the antecedent already stated in the sentence, the segment should read "that I was looking for" (or "which I was looking for"), not "what I was looking for".
◦ Corrected sentence: Hurray! Here is the toy that I was looking for as my birthday gift.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Hurray! Here is the toy" is grammatically correct; it simply introduces the antecedent noun "toy".

• Option 2: "No error" is incorrect because an error does exist, in the relative pronoun used in segment 3.

• Option 4: "as my birthday gift." is grammatically correct; it is a simple prepositional phrase with no error.

NOTE

• "What" is never preceded by a noun antecedent — it stands on its own, e.g. "I understood what he said" (no antecedent noun before "what").

• "That" can refer to both persons and things and is commonly used after superlatives, "all", "only", "the very", and when both a person and a thing are named together; "which" refers only to things/animals in non-defining clauses.

question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.
The politician was accused of accepting bribes and lied about it to the public.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. and lied about it.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "The politician was accused of accepting bribes and lied about it to the public" violates the rule of parallelism (parallel structure).

• Rule — Parallelism: When two or more actions are joined by a coordinating conjunction ("and") and share the same grammatical subject and construction, both actions must be expressed in the same grammatical form.

• Here, the first action is expressed as "accused of accepting" (a gerund, "accepting", governed by the preposition "of"); the second action, joined by "and", must therefore also be a gerund governed by "of" — "and of lying about it" — not the finite past-tense verb "lied".
◦ Corrected sentence: The politician was accused of accepting bribes and of lying about it to the public.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "of accepting bribes" is correct; it is the gerund phrase governed by "accused of".

• Option 2: "The politician was accused" is a correct, simple passive-voice opening to the sentence.

• Option 4: "to the public" is a correct prepositional phrase with no grammatical error.

NOTE

• Parallelism errors are common in SSC error-spotting questions wherever two verb forms are joined by "and", "or", "but", or "as well as" — always check that both sides of the conjunction match in form (both gerunds, both infinitives, or both finite verbs).

• Example of correct parallel structure: "She likes reading and writing" (not "reading and to write").

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Paragon
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Epitome.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Paragon" means a person or thing regarded as a perfect example of a particular quality; a model of excellence. (आदर्श, उत्कृष्ट उदाहरण)

• "Epitome" carries the same meaning — a perfect example or embodiment of a quality or type. (प्रतिरूप, आदर्श उदाहरण)
◦ Example: She is regarded as a paragon/epitome of honesty in her profession.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Transient (क्षणिक) — means lasting only for a short time, temporary; unrelated in meaning to "paragon".

• Option 3: Associate (सहयोगी) — means a partner or colleague; unrelated in meaning.

• Option 4: Grumpy (चिड़चिड़ा) — means bad-tempered and irritable; unrelated in meaning.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "paragon": model, ideal, exemplar, quintessence.

• Do not confuse "paragon" (a model of excellence) with "paradox" (a self-contradictory statement) — a common SSC distractor pairing.

question:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.
A.Through these experiences, Sarah gained a newfound appreciation for the beauty and complexity of the world, and returned home with a renewed sense of purpose and passion.
B.Sarah had always dreamed of traveling the world, but she never had the opportunity to do so until she graduated from college.
C.Along the way, she encountered a diverse array of individuals, each with their own unique stories and perspectives.
D.With her degree in hand, she set off on a backpacking adventure across Europe, eager to explore new cultures and meet new people.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. BDCA.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Sentence B is the opening/topic sentence — it introduces Sarah's long-held dream of travelling the world, which she could not pursue until she graduated.

• Sentence D logically follows B — "With her degree in hand" directly picks up on "until she graduated from college" in B, describing her setting off on her backpacking trip.

• Sentence C follows D — "Along the way" refers to the journey just introduced in D, describing the people she met during the trip.

• Sentence A is the concluding sentence — "Through these experiences" refers back to the encounters described in C, and it wraps up the paragraph with the outcome (renewed appreciation and purpose).
◦ Correct sequence: B → D → C → A, i.e., BDCA.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: BACD is incorrect because A (the concluding/summarising sentence) cannot appear immediately after the opening sentence B, before the journey (D) and the encounters (C) have even been described.

• Option 2: CBAD is incorrect because C ("Along the way") cannot open the paragraph — it presupposes a journey that has not yet been introduced.

• Option 3: DBCA is incorrect because D ("With her degree in hand, she set off") requires B's mention of graduation to have already been stated; D cannot precede B.

NOTE

• In paragraph-jumble questions, identify the topic sentence first (usually the one that introduces the subject with no dangling pronoun/reference), then trace logical/chronological connectors ("With her degree", "Along the way", "Through these experiences") to fix the sequence.

• Words like "this", "these", "such", "however", "therefore" are strong clues to a sentence's position, since they refer back to something already mentioned.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the bracketed word in the following sentence to fill in the blank.
The playwright borrowed the ________ (crux) of plot from Shakespeare.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. essence.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The bracketed word "crux" means the essential or most important point of a matter; the core or heart of something. (सार, मूल तत्व)

• "Essence" carries the same meaning — the fundamental, intrinsic nature or core of something. (सार, तत्व)
◦ Example: The playwright borrowed the essence of the plot from Shakespeare.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: peel (छिलका) — means the outer skin of a fruit or vegetable; unrelated in meaning.

• Option 2: subsistence (जीविका) — means the means of surviving or maintaining life at a minimal level; unrelated in meaning.

• Option 4: blueprint (खाका, योजना) — means a detailed plan or design; while related to "plan", it does not carry the specific sense of "core/essential point" that "crux" does.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "crux": core, gist, kernel, nucleus, nub.

• "Crux" is often paired in SSC vocabulary sets with "gist" and "essence" as near-synonyms, all meaning "the central point".

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
An imperfection; a blemish, a crack
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Flaw.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Flaw" means an imperfection, often concealed, that impairs soundness; a blemish or a crack. (दोष, खामी)
◦ Example: A small flaw in the diamond reduced its market value.

• A "flaw" can refer to a physical defect (a crack in glass) or an abstract shortcoming (a flaw in an argument or in someone's character).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Flaunt (दिखावा करना) — means to display something ostentatiously to attract attention; unrelated in meaning.

• Option 2: Fleck (धब्बा/छोटा कण) — means a small mark, streak, or particle (e.g., a fleck of dust); close in spelling but denotes a tiny spot, not an imperfection/crack.

• Option 4: Flea (पिस्सू) — a small jumping insect that feeds on blood; entirely unrelated in meaning.

NOTE

• Flaw/Fleck/Flaunt/Flea are commonly confused in SSC one-word-substitution and spelling questions due to their similar "Fl-" spelling pattern — always match the meaning carefully rather than the spelling alone.

• Related words: flawless (without imperfection), flawed (having defects).

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the underlined word in the given sentence.
He lost the golden opportunity due to his habit of procrastination.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. indecisiveness.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined word "procrastination" refers to the habit of delaying or postponing action, which typically arises from an inability to commit to a decision. (टाल-मटोल करने की आदत)

• Among the given options, "indecisiveness" — the inability to make decisions promptly — is the closest in sense, since a person's hesitation/indecision is the root cause of habitual delay (procrastination). (अनिर्णय की स्थिति)
◦ Example: He lost the golden opportunity due to his habit of indecisiveness.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: impulsiveness (आवेगशीलता) — means acting suddenly without thought; this is nearly the opposite tendency to procrastination (delaying action), not a synonym.

• Option 3: inquisitiveness (जिज्ञासा) — means excessive curiosity about things; unrelated to delaying decisions.

• Option 4: submissiveness (विनम्रता/अधीनता) — means readily yielding to the authority of others; unrelated to delaying decisions.

NOTE

• "Procrastination" is derived from Latin procrastinare ("pro-" = forward, "crastinus" = of tomorrow), literally "putting off until tomorrow".

• Related words often tested together: dilly-dallying, dawdling, and tardiness (all connected to delay), as opposed to promptness and punctuality.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the underlined word.
Syam does not intervene in others' affairs.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Meddle.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined word "intervene" means to become involved in a situation, especially to prevent or alter a result; to interfere in others' matters. (दखल देना)

• "Meddle" carries the same meaning — to interfere in something that is not one's concern, especially in an annoying way. (हस्तक्षेप करना)
◦ Example: Syam does not meddle in others' affairs.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Speak (बोलना) — a neutral verb meaning to talk; it does not carry the sense of interference.

• Option 3: Trouble (परेशान करना) — means to cause difficulty or worry to someone; not synonymous with interfering in matters.

• Option 4: Help (मदद करना) — means to assist; in fact nearly opposite in connotation to unwanted interference.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "intervene/meddle": interfere, intrude, tamper (with), poke one's nose (into) — the last being a common SSC idiom for meddling in others' affairs.

• "Intervene" is used positively in formal contexts (e.g., "the UN intervened to stop the conflict"), while "meddle" almost always carries a negative, unwelcome connotation.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the bracketed word in the following sentence to fill in the blank.
The text ___________ (implies) to several themes that need closer examination.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. alludes.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The bracketed word "implies" means to indirectly suggest or refer to something without stating it directly. (परोक्ष रूप से संकेत करना)

• "Alludes" carries the same meaning — to refer to something indirectly or in passing. (परोक्ष रूप से उल्लेख करना)
◦ Example: The text alludes to several themes that need closer examination.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: deceives (धोखा देना) — means to mislead someone by making them believe something false; unrelated in meaning.

• Option 3: embellishes (अलंकृत करना) — means to make something more attractive by adding decorative details, often exaggerating it; unrelated in meaning.

• Option 4: apprehends (समझना/गिरफ्तार करना) — means either to understand/grasp something or to arrest someone; unrelated to "implies".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "imply/allude": hint, insinuate, intimate, suggest.

• Distinguish "imply" (the speaker/writer suggests something) from "infer" (the listener/reader deduces something) — a classic SSC vocabulary trap.

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a spelling error.
According to a report / every day / thousands of animals / are slautered.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. are slautered.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The segment "are slautered" contains a spelling error: "slautered" is a misspelling of the correct word "slaughtered".

• Correct spelling: S-L-A-U-G-H-T-E-R-E-D. Note the letters "augh" in the middle (as in "daughter", "caught", "naughty") — these are commonly dropped or scrambled by candidates, as has happened here ("slautered" is missing the "gh").
◦ Corrected sentence: According to a report, every day, thousands of animals are slaughtered.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "thousands of animals" is spelled correctly; no error.

• Option 3: "every day" is spelled correctly; no error.

• Option 4: "According to a report" is spelled correctly; no error.

NOTE

• Other commonly misspelled "-augh-" words tested by SSC: daughter, caught, taught, naughty, slaughter, laughter.

• Always sound out the word syllable by syllable (slaugh-tered) to check whether the "augh" cluster has been dropped or altered — a frequent trick in SSC spelling-error questions.

question:
Select the most appropriate idiom for the underlined words in the given sentence.
Piyush is inexperienced in leather industry.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. a greenhorn.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined word "inexperienced" needs to be replaced with an idiom of equivalent meaning.

• The idiom "a greenhorn" means an inexperienced or naive person, a novice, especially one who is easily fooled. (अनुभवहीन व्यक्ति, नौसिखिया)
◦ Example: Piyush is a greenhorn in the leather industry.

• The term originates from the young, soft, "green" (immature) horns of young cattle, symbolising inexperience/youth.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: in great hands (अच्छे हाथों में) — means being taken care of by a capable or trustworthy person; unrelated to inexperience.

• Option 2: a sore thumb (नज़र में खटकने वाला) — used in the idiom "to stick out like a sore thumb", meaning to be conspicuously out of place; unrelated to inexperience.

• Option 3: hang fire (देरी होना/टलना) — means to delay or be postponed; unrelated to inexperience.

NOTE

• Other idioms meaning "inexperienced": "wet behind the ears", "a novice", "a fledgling" (a beginner in a particular activity).

• Idioms of experience (opposite sense): "an old hand", "a veteran", "know the ropes" (to be familiar with how something is done).

question:
Parts of a sentence are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the parts in the correct order to form a meaningful sentence.
(A) to simplify filling taxes
(B) to a single flat rate
(C) the current five rates
(D) by narrowing
(E) Forbes wanted
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. EADCB.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• (E) "Forbes wanted" must open the sentence, as it introduces the subject ("Forbes") and the main verb ("wanted") that governs the rest of the sentence.

• (A) "to simplify filling taxes" follows E directly, forming the infinitive object of "wanted" — "Forbes wanted to simplify filling taxes".

• (D) "by narrowing" follows A, introducing the means by which the simplification would be achieved.

• (C) "the current five rates" follows D, naming the object being narrowed.

• (B) "to a single flat rate" completes the sentence, stating what the five rates would be narrowed down to.
◦ Correct sentence: Forbes wanted to simplify filling taxes by narrowing the current five rates to a single flat rate.
◦ Correct sequence: E → A → D → C → B, i.e., EADCB.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: EBDCA is incorrect because (B) "to a single flat rate" cannot immediately follow (E) "Forbes wanted" — the object of "wanted" must be the infinitive phrase (A), not (B).

• Option 2: ECDAB is incorrect because (C) "the current five rates" cannot directly follow "Forbes wanted"; the infinitive "to simplify filling taxes" (A) must come first.

• Option 3: EDACB is incorrect because (D) "by narrowing" cannot come immediately after "Forbes wanted"; the infinitive object (A) must precede it.

NOTE

• In jumbled-sentence questions, first locate the part carrying the main subject + verb, then trace the logical chain: main verb → infinitive object → method/means ("by + gerund") → object of the means → final result.

• Phrases beginning with "to" (infinitives) usually follow the main verb directly when they act as its object, as seen here with "wanted to simplify".

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
She killed the cockroach.
option_1: The cockroach was being killed by her.
option_2: The cockroach is killed by her.
option_3: The cockroach was killed by her.
option_4: The cockroach has been killed by her.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The cockroach was killed by her.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "She killed the cockroach" is an assertive sentence in the Simple Past Tense.

• Rule — Simple Past Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + V2 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + was/were + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "the cockroach" becomes the subject; being singular, the auxiliary used is "was"; the verb "killed" (already V2/V3, as "kill" is a regular verb) is retained as the past participle; and "she" becomes the agent "her" after "by".
◦ Passive: The cockroach was killed by her.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "was being killed" is the passive form of the Past Continuous Tense, not the Simple Past Tense used in the original sentence.

• Option 2 is incorrect because "is killed" is the passive form of the Simple Present Tense, which changes the tense of the original sentence.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "has been killed" is the passive form of the Present Perfect Tense, again changing the tense of the original sentence.

NOTE

• The tense of the passive sentence must always match the tense of the active sentence — a very common SSC trap is offering passive options in the wrong tense.

• Regular verbs like "kill" have identical V2 and V3 forms (killed/killed); for irregular verbs (e.g., "break" → broke/broken), the V3 form must be used in the passive, not the V2 form.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
The student asked the teacher a question during class.
option_1: A question was asked by the student to the teacher during class.
option_2: A question is being asked by the student to the teacher during class.
option_3: A question asked by the student to the teacher during class.
option_4: A question will be asked by the student to the teacher during class.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. A question was asked by the student to the teacher during class.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "The student asked the teacher a question during class" is an assertive sentence in the Simple Past Tense, with the ditransitive verb "asked" taking two objects — the indirect object "the teacher" and the direct object "a question".

• Rule — Passive of Ditransitive Verbs: When a verb has both a direct and an indirect object, the direct object (here, "a question") is normally made the subject of the passive sentence, while the indirect object ("the teacher") follows the verb, introduced by an appropriate preposition ("to"/"for"), with the original subject becoming the agent after "by".
◦ Passive: A question was asked by the student to the teacher during class.

• The auxiliary "was" correctly matches the Simple Past Tense and the singular subject "a question"; the verb "ask" takes its past participle form "asked".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is incorrect because "is being asked" is the passive of the Present Continuous Tense, changing the tense of the original sentence.

• Option 3 is incorrect because it drops the auxiliary verb "was" altogether ("A question asked by..."), leaving the sentence without a finite verb — it is grammatically incomplete.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "will be asked" is the passive of the Simple Future Tense, changing the tense of the original sentence.

NOTE

• With ditransitive verbs like "give", "tell", "ask", "show", "teach", either object can technically become the subject of the passive, but SSC conventionally prefers making the direct object (the "thing" given/asked/told) the subject, as tested here.

• Always double check that the passive retains the exact tense and auxiliary appropriate to the original active sentence.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
People were ________ to safe places by the rescue team after the earthquake.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. evacuated.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct word required to fill the blank is "evacuated", meaning moved people away from a place of danger to a safer place.
◦ Example: People were evacuated to safe places by the rescue team after the earthquake.

• Correct spelling: E-V-A-C-U-A-T-E-D. The word is built from the Latin root evacuare ("e-" = out, "vacuare" = to empty), meaning literally "to empty out".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "ebacuated" — incorrect; the letter "v" has been wrongly replaced with "b".

• Option 3: "evkuated" — incorrect; the letter "a" after "v" has been dropped, and the "c" is missing.

• Option 4: "evakuated" — incorrect; the "c" has been wrongly replaced with "k".

NOTE

• Related words: evacuation (noun), evacuee (a person who has been evacuated).

• Similar-sounding words often confused in spelling tests: "vacate", "vacant", "vacuum" — all share the same Latin root "vacare/vacuus" meaning "empty".

question:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.
A)Electronic waste is a huge challenge to the world today.
B)But the unrequired purchase by consumers cannot be halted.
C)However, an awareness on reduce and reuse can be of great help.
D)Recycling industries are working hard to reduce the burden of waste.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. ADBC.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Sentence A is the topic sentence — it introduces the subject of the paragraph, "Electronic waste", as a global challenge.

• Sentence D follows A, describing one response to the challenge: recycling industries working hard to reduce the waste burden.

• Sentence B follows D, introduced by the contrasting connector "But", pointing out a limitation — that unnecessary consumer purchasing cannot be stopped (despite recycling efforts).

• Sentence C concludes the paragraph, introduced by "However", offering a solution — that awareness about reducing and reusing can help despite the limitation just mentioned in B.
◦ Correct sequence: A → D → B → C, i.e., ADBC.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: DBAC is incorrect because D ("Recycling industries are working hard...") cannot open the paragraph without A first establishing that electronic waste is a challenge.

• Option 2: ABCD is incorrect because C ("However, an awareness...") logically comes after B ("But the unrequired purchase..."), not before D; C's "However" must contrast with the limitation stated in B.

• Option 3: DABC is incorrect because D cannot precede A, for the same reason as in Option 1 — the topic (electronic waste as a challenge) must be introduced first.

NOTE

• Connector words such as "But" and "However" are key clues in paragraph-jumble questions — they signal a contrast with the immediately preceding idea, helping fix the correct sequence.

• Always identify the sentence that introduces the topic with no back-reference (here, A) as the starting point.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

All the housewives who went to the Kalpatharu Supermarket in Bengaluru had one great ambition: to be the lucky customer who did not have to pay for her (1)________ . For this was what that notice just inside the entrance promised. It said: 'Remember, once a week, one of our customers gets free goods. This may be your (2)________ day!'
For several weeks Mrs. Batliwala hoped, like many of her friends, to be the lucky (3)________ . Unlike her friends she never gave up hope. Her kitchen was full of things which she did not need. She dreamed of the day when the manager of the supermarket would approach her and say "Madam, this is your lucky day. (4)________ in your basket is free."
On Saturday morning, Mrs. Batliwala went to the supermarket and bought only tea. She went to the cash desk when the manager of the supermarket come up to her and said. "You are our lucky customer and everything in your basket is (5)________ !"

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. shopping.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Blank (1) requires a word denoting what a housewife does at a supermarket that she would ideally not have to pay for — the context is "to be the lucky customer who did not have to pay for her (1)________".

• "Shopping" fits perfectly, as the passage is set in a supermarket where customers pay for the goods (their "shopping") they buy.
◦ Completed: "...to be the lucky customer who did not have to pay for her shopping."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "cloths" does not fit the general context of a supermarket purchase covering all goods bought (groceries, tea, etc., as later mentioned), and is also not what the passage describes being paid for.

• Option 3: "sugar" is too specific an item; the passage is about the general bill for whatever the customer bought, not a single grocery item.

• Option 4: "jewellery" is not sold at a general supermarket like Kalpatharu, making it contextually inappropriate.

NOTE

• In cloze passages, always read the full surrounding sentence (and often the whole paragraph) before choosing an option — the correct word must fit both the grammar and the overall narrative logic of the passage.

• Here, the later reference to Mrs. Batliwala buying "only tea" and everything in her "basket" being free confirms that blank (1) refers to her general shopping/purchases, not one specific item.

◦ Completed: "This may be your lucky day!"

• Option 3: "smart" is irrelevant to the context of winning free goods by chance.

• Option 4: "happy" is a plausible-sounding general word, but it does not carry the specific sense of chance/good fortune that the context (getting free goods once a week) demands — "lucky" is the precise fit, and is echoed later in the passage ("to be the lucky customer", "you are our lucky customer").

NOTE

• The word "lucky" recurs throughout this passage ("lucky customer", "lucky day") — in cloze passages, repeated key words elsewhere in the text are a strong clue to the intended answer for a blank.

• Always cross-check a chosen option against the passage's recurring theme or vocabulary.

• "Everything" fits perfectly, matching the passage's climax later on, where the manager actually says, "everything in your basket is free."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 4: "packets" narrows the meaning to only packaged goods, which does not match the intended all-inclusive sense confirmed later in the passage ("everything in your basket is free").

NOTE

• The passage later repeats this exact sentence almost verbatim at the climax ("everything in your basket is (5)________!"), directly confirming that blank (4) must also be "everything".

• Cloze passages frequently repeat or paraphrase key sentences near the end to build toward a climax — spotting this repetition is a reliable shortcut to the correct answer.

solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. free.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Blank (5) appears in the passage's climax: "You are our lucky customer and everything in your basket is (5)________!"

• "Free" fits perfectly, completing the story's punchline — Mrs. Batliwala, who bought only tea, turns out to be the lucky customer whose entire (small) basket of goods costs nothing.
◦ Completed: "...everything in your basket is free!"

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "yours" does not make sense here — the goods were already hers by virtue of being in her basket; the surprise/reward being announced is that she does not have to pay, i.e., they are free.

• Option 2: "expensive" contradicts the entire premise of the passage, which is about winning free goods, not being told they cost more.

• Option 3: "cheap" is close in spirit but does not match the passage's established premise of goods being entirely free ("did not have to pay", "gets free goods"), not merely inexpensive.

NOTE

• The passage explicitly establishes the premise "gets free goods" near the start; the ending must be consistent with this, confirming "free" as the answer, not merely "cheap".

• There is also a touch of situational irony here: after weeks of hoping for something big, Mrs. Batliwala wins on the one day she buys "only tea" — a good example of how SSC comprehension passages test overall narrative understanding, not just vocabulary.
